title: Emergence of Propagating Exciton-Polaritons in Hybrid Waveguide-van der Waals Heterostructures
authors: Alina Schubert, Karoline Becker, Andreas Thies, Rico Schwartz, Takashi Taniguchi, Kenji Watanabe, Henije Stolz, Alexander Szameit, Matthias Heinrich, Tobias Korn
abstract: Integrating few-layer materials into photonic circuits is a promising concept for novel on-chip photonic applications. We incorporate transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) with femtosecond-laser-written surface waveguides, which are embedded in fused silica chips. Our novel low-temperature optical spectroscopy setup enables coupling to the waveguide and simultaneous focus from the top to the TMD layer for a distinct excitation and collection of micro-photoluminescence ($μ$PL) signals in several measurement geometries. Along these lines, we observe spectral changes of the A exciton for encapsulated TMD monolayers when capturing the $μ$PL signal propagating through the waveguide. Depending on the thickness of the encapsulation with hexagonal boron nitride (hBN), these changes manifest as energetic redshifts of the A exciton, or even a splitting of the A exciton into two components. We attribute this behavior to strong coupling of the waveguide mode and the exciton in the sample, giving rise to the formation of propagating exciton-polaritons. Our interpretation is supported by calculations for a simplified model of a slab waveguide in the vicinity of an exciton by using the transfer matrix method. Having proven to be a highly adaptable framework for the study of propagating polaritons, our experimental platform likewise holds great promise for harnessing the unique properties of exciton-polaristons in integrated photonic circuits.
summary: Researchers demonstrate the formation of propagating exciton-polaritons by integrating TMD monolayers into photonic waveguides. They use low-temperature spectroscopy to observe characteristic spectral splittings in the A exciton, confirming strong coupling between excitons and the waveguide mode. The findings are supported by detailed theoretical modeling using transfer matrix methods, advancing on-chip quantum light sources.
main_problem: The research investigates the emergence and properties of propagating exciton-polaritons formed by coupling excitons within Transition Metal Dichalcogenides (TMDs) to optical waveguide modes.
main_result: Strong coupling leads to observable spectral shifts, redshifts, or splittings in the A exciton resonance, confirming the formation of hybrid exciton-polaritons whose properties can be modeled theoretically.
method: The study employs a combination of low-temperature optical spectroscopy ($\mu$PL) measurements across various geometries and theoretical modeling using the transfer matrix method for waveguide dispersion relations.
model_or_system: The physical system is a hybrid structure comprising TMD monolayers (e.g., MoSe2, WSe2) encapsulated by hBN, placed atop femtosecond-laser-written surface waveguides embedded in fused silica chips.
key_observables: Spectral shifts/splittings of the A exciton ($\Delta E$), polariton energy levels (upper and lower branches), group velocity ($v_g$), and propagation distance ($l$).
important_parameters: hBN encapsulation thickness, temperature (down to 4 K), waveguide width, and material-specific exciton/trion energies.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that observed peak splitting is due to strong coupling; theoretical models are highly simplified approximations used to highlight physical trends rather than predict exact values.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the hybrid structure schematic, $\mu$PL spectra showing polarization and temperature dependence of exciton/polariton features, and theoretical dispersion relations derived from transfer matrix calculations.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the experimental platform and observing spectral anomalies (splitting/redshift) in TMDs. This observation is then theoretically modeled using waveguide theory to confirm the polaritonic nature, followed by detailed analysis of temperature and geometry dependence.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses open quantum systems dynamics in solid-state photonics, providing experimental evidence and theoretical frameworks for engineered light-matter coupling (exciton-photon interaction) crucial for integrated quantum devices.
